title: The Second Passover and the Cloud That Leads
summary: A year after leaving Egypt, Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai. Some men who are unclean from contact with a dead body ask why they should be shut out, and God answers by providing a second Passover a month later for anyone unclean or far away, while warning that those who simply neglect it will be cut off, and welcoming foreigners who wish to keep it. The chapter then describes the cloud over the tabernacle, which by its lifting and settling tells Israel when to march and when to camp.
story: Like chapter 7, this chapter reaches back before the census of Numbers 1:1. The Passover falls on the fourteenth day of the first month, the first anniversary of the night Israel left Egypt. Before the people leave Sinai, they remember how they came to be free. The chapter's two halves face backward and forward. The Passover looks back to the exodus; the cloud looks ahead to the road. When the cloud lifts in the next chapter, Israel will follow it into the wilderness, and this chapter has already told the reader how that following is meant to work: at the LORD's command they camp, and at the LORD's command they set out.
historical:
This is the only Passover the Torah records Israel keeping during the wilderness years. The next one mentioned is at Gilgal after the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 5:10), where the men born in the wilderness were first circumcised. The provision for a second Passover in the second month was used centuries later. When King Hezekiah invited all Israel to Jerusalem, the Passover was held “in the second month” because not enough priests had consecrated themselves and the people had not gathered in time (2 Chronicles 30:2-3). Jewish tradition still marks the date, on the fourteenth of the second month, as Pesach Sheni, the Second Passover.

The cloud was already familiar from Exodus, where it led Israel out of Egypt as a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21-22) and filled the tabernacle when it was completed (Exodus 40:34-38). Numbers repeats and expands that description because the march is about to begin, and the cloud will decide its every stage.
cultural:
Passover was a family meal of lamb, unleavened bread, and bitter herbs, eaten at twilight in memory of the night the LORD struck Egypt's firstborn and passed over Israel's houses marked with blood (Exodus 12). It had strict rules: none of the lamb could be left until morning, and none of its bones could be broken (verse 12). Taking part required ritual cleanness, and contact with a corpse made a person unclean for seven days. In a society where families washed and buried their own dead, someone would often be in that state through no fault of their own.

The foreigner in verse 14 is the ger, a resident alien who lived among Israel without belonging to its tribes. Exodus 12:48 had already allowed such people to keep Passover if the males of their household were circumcised, and this chapter repeats that one law applies to foreigner and native alike. In the ancient world, where religion was usually tied to birth and nation, the principle is remarkable: the central festival of Israel's identity was open to outsiders who chose to join.
literary: The first half of the chapter is a case story of a kind found several times in Numbers (see also 15:32-36, 27:1-11, and 36:1-12): a situation the law has not covered arises, people bring it to Moses, Moses waits for God's answer, and a new ruling follows. It shows Israel's law as living instruction from a present God, not a closed code. The second half is built on heavy repetition. The phrase “at the LORD's command” (literally at the mouth of the LORD) appears seven times in verses 18-23, and the verbs set out and camp alternate again and again. The effect is to make the reader feel the unpredictability of the cloud, lingering two days, a month, or longer, and the single rule that governed it all: Israel moved when God moved.

outline.t: Passover kept at Sinai on its appointed day
The question of those unclean from a dead body
The second Passover, the warning, and the foreigner
The cloud over the tabernacle directs the march

doctrines.note: The cloud settles and lifts on no schedule Israel could predict, sometimes for a night, sometimes for a month. God's guidance is real and specific, but it does not come as a timetable. The people's part is to watch and follow.

Passover is a meal commanded by God to remember and share in his saving act. The chapter shows the seriousness of such a meal: God makes room for those kept away through no fault of their own, but those who neglect it on purpose are cut off. Christians have long read the Lord's Supper against this background.
Verse 14 opens Passover to the resident foreigner under the same statute as the native Israelite. From the start, Israel's worship had a door for outsiders who chose to join God's people.

words.note: Pesach, Passover. The noun names both the festival and the lamb eaten at it, and it is connected with the verb for the LORD passing over Israel's houses in Exodus 12. It is the festival of Israel's birth as a free people, and the Gospels place Jesus' death at Passover.

Moed, appointed time. It is the same word used in the name Tent of Meeting, the appointed place of meeting, and it names Israel's festivals as fixed times set by God. The unclean men's complaint in verse 7 is that they will miss the appointed time. God's answer creates a second appointed time for them.

Ger, a sojourner or resident foreigner. The ger lived among Israel without tribal land or kin. Israel was repeatedly reminded that they had been sojourners in Egypt, and the law protected such people. Verse 14 extends Passover to them under one statute for all.

Anan, cloud. It is the visible sign of God's presence over the tabernacle, appearing like fire at night. The word appears eleven times in verses 15-23, and the whole march of Israel depends on it. Later Scripture uses the cloud for God's presence at the dedication of Solomon's temple and at the transfiguration of Jesus.

christ: The Passover rule that none of the lamb's bones be broken (verse 12, following Exodus 12:46) is quoted by John at the cross. When the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs, John writes that this happened “so that the Scripture would be fulfilled” and cites the words “Not one of His bones will be broken” (John 19:36). Paul makes the connection explicit: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The second Passover, made for people who would otherwise be excluded, fits the Gospel pattern of a table widened for the unclean and the distant, and the welcome of the foreigner anticipates Paul's words to Gentile believers that “you are no longer strangers and foreigners” (Ephesians 2:19). The cloud reappears at the transfiguration, when “a voice came from the cloud” and said, “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” (Luke 9:35). Israel followed the cloud; the disciples are told to follow the Son.

hard.q: What does it mean that someone who neglects Passover will be cut off from his people?
hard.a: The phrase appears often in the priestly laws, and its meaning is debated. One view takes it as a death penalty carried out by the community. Another, argued by Jacob Milgrom among others, holds that it is a punishment God himself carries out, such as early death or the ending of a person's family line, since in some passages God says, “I will set My face against that man and cut him off from his people” (Leviticus 20:3). A third view sees it as exclusion from the covenant community, something like excommunication. Many interpreters think the phrase could cover more than one of these. What is clear in this chapter is the contrast. The men who were unclean through no fault of their own receive a second chance; the man who is clean and able but simply does not bother is judged. The warning falls on contempt, not on circumstance.

questions: The unclean men did not accept being left out; they asked, and God made a way. What does their question teach about bringing hard cases to God?
The cloud sometimes stayed a night and sometimes a month. How do you respond when God's timing is not what you expected or planned?
Passover was open to foreigners who chose to join Israel. Who might feel like an outsider in your community of faith, and how could the door be opened wider?
